result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.add_circulant_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Add a circulant graph to the current graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L7239-L7360){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.add_circulant_graph( n, offsets, type=None, label=True, rel=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Circulant graph](/assets/graphs/add-circulant-graph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Three circulant graphs on the same ring of eight nodes. With offsets 1 each node joins its two ring neighbors, giving a cycle; offsets 1 and 2 add the chords that skip one node; offsets 1 and 3 instead add chords that skip two. Every node has the same number of neighbors, twice the number of offsets." width="100%"} Places `n` nodes on a ring and joins each node `i` to node `(i + o) mod n` for every offset `o` in `offsets=`. Offsets `1` give the cycle, offsets `1` and `2` the ring lattice that small-world models start from, and offsets `1` to `n // 2` the complete graph. Every node looks the same, so circulant graphs are regular and vertex-transitive. In an undirected graph the offsets `o` and `n - o` describe the same edges, so each pair is joined only once; with `n` even, the offset `n / 2` joins each node to the one directly opposite. In a directed graph every offset gives its own edge `i -> (i + o) mod n`, so `[1]` is a directed cycle and `[1, n - 1]` adds the reverse cycle as well. Nodes are created in ring order. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Circulant graphs are useful for: - modeling ring networks with fixed-length shortcuts (chordal rings, interconnection networks for parallel computers) - building regular test graphs of any even degree, or the starting lattice of a Watts-Strogatz model before rewiring - examples in algebraic graph theory, since their spectrum has a closed form ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes on the ring. Must be at least `2`. [offsets]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Ring distances to join, e.g. `[1, 3]`. Each offset is taken modulo `n=` and must not be a multiple of `n=` (which would give a self-loop). Repeated or equivalent offsets add no extra edges. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string; a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `n=` is less than `2`, `offsets=` is empty, or an offset is a multiple of `n=`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} With offsets `1` and `3`, each of the eight nodes is joined to the nodes one and three steps away in both directions, so every node has degree `4`: ::: {#e940a5e8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_circulant_graph(n=8, offsets=[1, 3]) graph.count_edges(), {graph.get_degree(nid) for nid in graph.get_node_ids()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (16, {4}) ``` ::: ::: The offset `4` in an eight-node ring joins opposite nodes, so each pair appears once and adds only one to every degree. Together with offset `1` this gives the Möbius ladder on eight nodes (the Wagner graph): ::: {#e3f531ad .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} wagner = ec.Graph().add_circulant_graph(n=8, offsets=[1, 4]) wagner.count_edges(), {wagner.get_degree(nid) for nid in wagner.get_node_ids()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (12, {3}) ``` ::: ::: In a directed graph each offset gives one edge per node, all pointing the same way around the ring: ::: {#a83fe326 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph(directed=True).add_circulant_graph(n=4, offsets=[1]).get_edges_str_repr( use_labels=True ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['1->2', '2->3', '3->4', '4->1'] ``` ::: :::
